newsitem.title: UK: Pressure builds for UK Jan rate rise after M4 data.
newsitem.headline: Pressure builds for UK Jan rate rise after M4 data.

text.p: A sharp acceleration in UK broad money supply in November completes this week's collection of strong economic data and will increase pressure on Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to raise interest rates in January.
"This is further ammunition for the Bank of England. The data will make it very hard for Clarke to resist the Bank's call for higher rates in January," said Adam Cole, UK economist at James Capel.
M4 grew 10.8 percent in the year to November compared with 10.3 percent in October.
The money supply data come a day after other figures showed a record 95,800 fall in unemployment in November coupled with a 0.7 percent rise in retail sales in the month.
"The UK financial data put yet more pressure on the Chancwellor to hike rates at the next monetary meeting," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at Bank of America.
"The much stronger-than-expected surge in M4 combined with the buoyancy of yesterday's real side statistics all but guarantee the Bank will call for another tightening."
A consensus view is growing that Clarke will bite the bullet and raise rates by a quarter point after the January 15 meeting.

M4 acquired a reputation in the late 1980s for signalling future inflationary pressures. But in recent years, it has been distorted by a number of factors, in particular merger activity in the financial sector, which has called into question its usefulness.

In November, M4 lending was again swollen by heavy corporate borrowing which is not seen as carrying the same inflation threat as the personal sector. "Nevertheless, the personal sector itself posted another large increase consistent with strong retail sales in the month, and is probably indicative of more to come," said Hawkins.
A breakdown which covers part of the M4 lending figures from the British Bankers' Association showed the rise in personal sector lending and consumer credit eased in November, but remains robust.
Lending to the services and financial sector rose strongly.
Other data covering mortgage approvals show that demand for home loans remained strong in November.
Net mortgage approvals were 3.651 billion stg, slightly below the 3.967 billion seen in Ocotbner.
Some economists said the data show the first signs that the base rate rise on October 30 may be beginning to bite.

"This data provides tentative signs that the rate rise may have already started to dampen mortgage demand, both through the withdrawal of many attractive fixed-rate packages and, more importantly, through higher rate expectations," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
She noted the annual growth of the volume of net new approvals fell from 33 percent in October to 13 percent in November.
